PullRequest.Title: Registers @vscode/markdown-editor in markdown-language-features extension

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The changed callback, full-string observable read, JSON webview transport, full-range WorkspaceEdit, and uncoalesced async call path are all directly traced in repository code. Exact latency varies with file size and typing rate, but the O(document size) cost per mutation is not speculative.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Full-document strings, JSON serialization bytes, extension-host/main-thread IPC calls, and whole-document text-edit CPU/allocation
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For a document of N characters and E editor mutations, the bridge transfers and compares O(N×E) text and applies E full-range WorkspaceEdits; rapid typing can also leave multiple async applyEdit calls in flight because the message callback is not sequenced or coalesced.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Increased typing latency, extension-host/main-thread CPU and GC pressure, and excessive IPC for large Markdown files
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR there was no editable Markdown webview bridge, so typing did not serialize the entire document through a webview message and submit a full-range WorkspaceEdit for every source mutation.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new autorun reads the complete sourceText and the callback on this line posts that complete string for every model change. The provider then calls document.getText() for comparison and replaces Range(0,0..lineCount,0) with the full payload through workspace.applyEdit.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 102 explicitly sends `{ type: 'edit', content: text }`, where `text` is the complete model source read by the new autorun, creating the per-mutation full-document bridge that did not exist before this diff.
Findings.Title: Send incremental edits instead of full documents
Findings.Impact: Typing in the experimental editor for a realistically large Markdown file performs document-sized serialization and a whole-document bulk edit per keystroke, directly on the input critical path. A burst of keystrokes can queue overlapping document-sized edits and make the editor lag or churn CPU/GC.
Findings.Evidence: editor.ts:83-86 invokes onEdit with model.sourceText.value whenever the observable changes, and line 102 sends that full value. markdownEditorProvider.ts:50-62 compares against another full document string, constructs a replacement spanning the entire document, and calls workspace.applyEdit. Core webview transport JSON.stringify's messages in mainThreadWebviews.ts:79-82/extHostWebviewMessaging.ts:22-64, and applyEdit crosses to MainThreadBulkEdits through extHostBulkEdits.ts:31-34.
Findings.Recommendation: Transport and apply the actual changed range (or a minimal diff against the last acknowledged text) as an incremental WorkspaceEdit. Sequence/coalesce pending edits so rapid input cannot accumulate concurrent full-document work.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The retention flag and API lifecycle contract directly prove the memory lifetime, and the new init protocol proves the document state is reconstructible. Exact bytes depend on tab/document size, so severity is medium rather than high.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Hidden webview iframes, Markdown source/model and parse objects, rendered DOM and Mermaid SVG nodes, and loaded editor/Mermaid JavaScript heaps
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Retained memory grows with the number of opened-but-hidden custom-editor tabs and with each document's text, rendered node count, and diagrams; there is no eviction before a panel is closed.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Sustained renderer memory growth and greater GC pressure across normal tab switching sessions
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this provider was registered, opening Markdown files did not create these editor webviews, and the default custom-webview lifecycle would destroy hidden HTML contexts rather than retain them.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The registration now opts every Markdown editor panel into `retainContextWhenHidden`, preserving the full iframe and editor state after the user switches tabs even though the implementation can reconstruct itself from the authoritative TextDocument on its existing ready/init handshake.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 53 changes the custom editor from the default destroy-when-hidden lifecycle to retaining each complete webview context in the background.
Findings.Title: Release hidden Markdown editor webviews
Findings.Impact: A user who opens several large Markdown files in the experimental editor and then moves among tabs keeps every hidden editor's model, full rendered DOM, and heavyweight webview modules resident until the tabs are closed, increasing VS Code renderer memory and GC overhead.
Findings.Evidence: The added option on line 53 retains hidden contexts. vscode.d.ts:10055-10077 explicitly documents that this has high memory overhead and should only be used when context cannot be quickly saved/restored. Here markdownEditorProvider.ts:44-46 already sends the complete authoritative TextDocument whenever a context posts `ready`, and editor.ts:104-123 rebuilds the editor from that init; getState/setState are unused. The adjacent `supportsMultipleEditorsPerDocument` option also permits more retained contexts.
Findings.Recommendation: Remove `retainContextWhenHidden`; persist only compact view state such as selection/scroll if needed and rebuild from TextDocument on the existing ready/init path.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The event frequency, available incremental ranges, full getText payload, JSON transport, and full StringValue reset are directly traced. The exact render cost inside the package is not required to prove the O(document size) serialization/allocation regression and only affects magnitude.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Full-document string allocations and JSON IPC bytes, followed by full editor-model resets and Markdown render work in the webview
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For a document of N characters and E external/source-editor changes, each matching custom editor sends O(N×E) text instead of the usually small `contentChanges`; the cost also multiplies by the number of live custom-editor views for that document.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Excessive IPC, CPU/GC pressure, and slower synchronized editing for large Markdown files
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR there was no custom Markdown editor listener forwarding TextDocument changes into a webview, so normal source edits did not trigger this document-sized message and model reset.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new onDidChangeTextDocument handler ignores the event's incremental `contentChanges`, calls document.getText(), and posts the entire current document. The webview handles every message by constructing a new full StringValue and setting model.sourceText.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 75 converts every incremental TextDocumentChangeEvent into a full-document `update` message, introducing document-sized synchronization work per external change.
Findings.Title: Forward text-document patches instead of full snapshots
Findings.Impact: When a large Markdown document is changed outside this webview—for example while the source editor and experimental editor are open side by side—every keystroke or formatter edit serializes the full file across the extension-host/webview boundary and resets the webview model, causing lag and allocation churn.
Findings.Evidence: The added handler at lines 71-75 sends `document.getText()` for every matching event. vscode.d.ts:13411-13462 shows the event already provides range/offset/length/text patches. editor.ts:109-117 receives the snapshot and creates a new StringValue for the complete content. ExtHostWebview.postMessage serializes every payload with JSON.stringify before IPC (extHostWebview.ts:129-134 and extHostWebviewMessaging.ts:22-64).
Findings.Recommendation: Serialize `e.contentChanges` as ordered range/offset patches and apply corresponding StringEdits in the webview; coalesce batches while preserving the event's edit ordering.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The static import, unconditional initialization, single-bundle build settings, and Mermaid-only call site are directly visible. Bundle byte size is not measured, so magnitude is reflected as medium severity, but the eager critical-path mechanism is certain.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Bundled JavaScript bytes plus browser parse, compile, initialization, and module-heap work for Mermaid and its D3/Cytoscape/layout dependency graph
Findings.PerformanceScaling: The fixed Mermaid bundle and initialization cost is paid once for every newly created Markdown editor webview, regardless of whether the document contains zero Mermaid blocks; it grows further with simultaneously retained editor contexts.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Slower custom-editor first paint and increased CPU/memory for ordinary Markdown documents
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR, opening a Markdown document in this new editor did not load Mermaid or its dependency graph; Mermaid-specific work in the existing dedicated extension is scoped to Mermaid rendering surfaces.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new webview entrypoint statically imports Mermaid and initializes it at module evaluation, before the document is received and even when renderCustomCodeBlock never encounters a Mermaid block.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 8 places the Mermaid package in the unconditional editor entry module, and added line 13 initializes it before any content or code-block language is examined.
Findings.Title: Load Mermaid only when a diagram is rendered
Findings.Impact: Every user who opens the experimental editor—including for plain Markdown—must load and evaluate Mermaid's large renderer graph before the editor is ready, delaying first paint and consuming heap for functionality most documents do not use.
Findings.Evidence: Line 8 is a top-level static import and editor.ts:13 immediately initializes it; the only consumer is the `language === 'mermaid'` branch at lines 63-80. esbuild-webview-common.mts:11-19 bundles and minifies a single ESM entry without splitting, while the lockfile shows Mermaid bringing D3, Cytoscape, dagre, layout, parser, and related packages into this bundle.
Findings.Recommendation: Split Mermaid into a separate webview chunk/entry and initialize it lazily on the first `mermaid` code block, caching the resulting module promise for subsequent diagrams.

Scenarios.Scenario: Activate the built-in Markdown extension without opening the experimental custom editor
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Provider registration runs during the extension's existing activation path; no Markdown editor webview, document parsing, Mermaid evaluation, or document synchronization must complete for activation itself.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One provider registration per extension activation.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Synchronous registration only; no queue, limiter, or repeated per-document work is started.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache is consulted. The editor bundle and local resources remain unloaded until a custom editor is opened.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: extension.shared.ts only imports the lightweight provider class and registers it; Mermaid is imported by the separate webview entrypoint.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Registration overhead is trivial; bundle packaging increases install artifacts but not this runtime path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable activation regression; the expensive editor dependencies are not executed on this scenario.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open an ordinary Markdown file in the experimental custom editor
Scenarios.CriticalPath: VS Code must create the webview, load/parse editor.js and editor.css, run module initialization, exchange ready/init with the extension host, parse the full Markdown source, and construct the editor DOM before the editor is usable.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Load bundled editor.js, editor.css, fonts, and emitted local assets through webview resource URLs
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At least the script and stylesheet per cold webview, plus referenced font/assets; browser caching may reduce physical reads on warm opens.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The experimental editor and its resources did not exist before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The script and stylesheet are required before the custom editor can render.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send the complete TextDocument from extension host to the webview in the init message
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One document-sized payload per created/recreated webview context.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The webview cannot construct its model and view until this payload arrives.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Bundle, parse, compile, and initialize Mermaid and its renderer dependency graph as part of editor.js
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Once per new webview even when the document has zero Mermaid blocks.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Opening this editor did not load Mermaid because the editor did not exist.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Static import evaluation occurs before ready/init processing and therefore delays first usable render.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One webview per opened editor; document text and rendered node count scale with file size. Mermaid's fixed dependency graph is loaded even when the effective Mermaid-block cardinality is zero.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Resource loads may overlap in the browser, but module evaluation and editor construction are on the webview's first-paint critical path. No lazy gate excludes Mermaid for non-Mermaid documents.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Browser/resource caches can make subsequent local asset reads warm, but each new webview context still evaluates the bundled module and initializes Mermaid. No negative cache avoids Mermaid when the document has no diagrams.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: top-level import/initialization and the single bundled ESM build are directly traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The generated editor.js byte size and exact milliseconds were not supplied, but the static import and unsplit esbuild configuration make the eager critical-path work certain.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable eager-work regression: ordinary Markdown pays the full Mermaid startup cost.

Scenarios.Scenario: Render Markdown containing Mermaid code blocks
Scenarios.CriticalPath: After the document model identifies each Mermaid code block, Mermaid parsing/layout/rendering must complete asynchronously before that block shows its SVG; the rest of the editor can initially render without waiting for each promise.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Parse, lay out, and generate SVG for each Mermaid block
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One render invocation per Mermaid block encountered by the editor view; further calls on updates were not established from available package source.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The new editor had no Mermaid block renderer before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the editor's initial synchronous path after the placeholder div is returned, but on the per-diagram completion path.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number and complexity of Mermaid blocks; layout cost grows with diagram nodes/edges.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each renderCustomCodeBlock starts a Mermaid render promise immediately; no limiter or cancellation is visible in the changed code. The package's behavior on incremental view updates is not available, so repeated-render multiplicity was not assumed.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The Mermaid module is already eagerly loaded. No diagram-result cache is implemented; failures fall back to source text and are not negatively cached.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for initial per-block rendering, lower for rerender frequency; only the certain eager module cost was reported.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Diagram complexity can vary widely, and package update behavior is unavailable; no separate concurrency finding was submitted without proof of repeated invocation.
Scenarios.Verdict: Initial diagram rendering is feature-required. No additional finding beyond eager loading was submitted.

Scenarios.Scenario: Type in the experimental Markdown editor
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Each model source mutation runs the autorun, materializes the complete source string, posts it from the webview to the extension host, compares it with another full TextDocument string, then submits a full-range WorkspaceEdit over extension-host/main-thread RPC before the authoritative document reflects the edit.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Serialize and send the complete Markdown source from webview to extension host
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One document-sized message per sourceText mutation, including an immediate redundant autorun after init.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required before the authoritative TextDocument can be updated, so it is on the input synchronization path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Convert the full-range WorkspaceEdit and invoke MainThreadBulkEdits over extension-host RPC
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One full-document text edit per non-identical webview edit, with multiple calls potentially outstanding during fast typing.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Typing in the standard text editor applies native incremental edits rather than this webview/full-document bulk-edit path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The TextDocument, dirty state, and native undo/redo do not advance until this work applies.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Document size N and edit count E; total transferred/processed text is O(N×E), typically one round trip and one full-range bulk edit per keystroke.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The onDidReceiveMessage listener is async but event delivery does not sequence or coalesce returned promises, so rapid mutations can have multiple workspace.applyEdit calls outstanding. There is no shared limiter or latest-value queue.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cached document hash, incremental patch state, or coalescing is used. The equality check itself materializes and scans full text; identical initial content only avoids applyEdit after a redundant full round trip.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: all message, serialization, and bulk-edit stages are visible in changed and transitive code.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact lag depends on document size, renderer speed, and typing rate, but document-sized serialization and bulk-edit work per mutation are directly established.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable high-severity repeated-work and missing-coalescing regression.

Scenarios.Scenario: Edit the same Markdown TextDocument outside the custom webview while the experimental editor is live
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Every matching TextDocumentChangeEvent obtains the complete current document, serializes it from extension host to webview, and replaces the webview model's sourceText with a new full StringValue before the synchronized custom view is current.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: JSON-serialize and post the complete document from extension host to each matching live webview
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One N-character message per matching document event per live custom view, without grouping or coalescing.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: On the synchronized custom-editor update path; side-by-side editing waits on webview model/render work to display the new state.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Allocate a new full StringValue and reset the editor model from the snapshot
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One full-document model reset per delivered update message.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required before the custom view can represent the external change.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Document size N, external edit events E, and live custom views K for the document; transfer/allocation is O(N×E×K), whereas event.contentChanges normally contains small patches.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Updates are posted immediately per event and per wired panel. There is no debounce, ordered patch queue, or coalescing; webview message delivery provides the effective sequencing.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No snapshot hash or patch cache is used. A retained hidden context remains live for message posting according to the Webview API, though scripts may be suspended while hidden.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high for full snapshot serialization and allocation; render cost was not needed for the finding.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The markdown-editor package's internal rerender granularity is unavailable, so only proven full-string IPC/allocation costs were used.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable document-snapshot fan-out; incremental event patches are already available.

Scenarios.Scenario: Switch away from several opened experimental Markdown editor tabs
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Tab switching itself does not wait for cleanup because the PR opts out of destroying hidden contexts; the retained contexts remain off the immediate UI critical path but continue consuming renderer memory until panels close.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of hidden editor tabs and each document's source/model size, rendered DOM nodes, diagram SVGs, and loaded module heap.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: No cleanup, eviction, or bounded cache runs when panels become hidden. Disposal only occurs when each WebviewPanel is closed.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: retainContextWhenHidden effectively acts as an unbounded per-panel live-context cache. There is no eviction policy; the existing ready/init protocol could recreate content from TextDocument if contexts were released.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: the retention flag and lifecycle contract directly establish object lifetime.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact retained bytes depend on file/render complexity and shared browser module behavior, but WebviewPanelOptions explicitly documents high memory overhead.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable unbounded-retention regression for normal multi-tab workflows.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 10 changed files and every package-lock diff page. Submitted four findings covering both full-document synchronization directions, unconditional Mermaid startup work, and retained hidden webview memory. No concrete shipped-regression fix was present, so no blame/regression-fix record was applicable.
